overview: dbt (data build tool) is a transformation framework that lets analytics engineers write data transformations as SQL SELECT statements, which dbt turns into tables and views inside a cloud data warehouse.

dbt owns the 'T' in ELT (Extract, Load, Transform): raw data is first loaded into the warehouse by ingestion tools, and dbt transforms it in place using the warehouse's own compute, rather than pulling data out to a separate transformation engine.

Beyond running SQL, dbt adds software-engineering discipline to analytics: version control, modularity through ref(), automated testing, documentation, and a dependency graph (DAG) that orders and parallelizes model builds.
learningObjectives: Explain what dbt is and how it fits into a modern ELT pipeline on a cloud data warehouse.
Distinguish ELT from ETL and articulate why warehouse-native transformation became the standard.
Describe how dbt compiles SQL SELECTs into managed tables/views and why that brings engineering rigor to analytics.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: dbt is an open-source command-line tool and transformation framework that enables analytics engineers to define data transformations as modular SQL SELECT statements (models) plus YAML configuration. dbt compiles these models (resolving Jinja templating such as ref() and source()), computes a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of dependencies, and executes the resulting DDL/DML (CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT) against a target data warehouse. It implements the Transform stage of ELT, layering version control, testing, documentation, and reproducible builds on top of warehouse-native SQL.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of dbt as a smart recipe manager for your data. You write each transformation as a simple SELECT query that says 'here is the clean data I want,' and dbt figures out how to build it as a real table in your warehouse. It reads all your recipes, works out which one depends on which (you can't bake the cake before mixing the batter), builds them in the right order, and checks the results with tests. In ELT, the raw ingredients are already dumped into the warehouse; dbt is the kitchen that turns them into finished dishes right there, using the warehouse's own oven instead of carrying everything to a separate kitchen.
coreConcept.historicalContext: dbt was created by Fishtown Analytics (now dbt Labs) around 2016, at the moment cloud data warehouses like Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, and later Snowflake made warehouse compute cheap and elastic. Traditional ETL tools (Informatica, SSIS) transformed data in external engines before loading it, because older on-premise warehouses were expensive to compute on. When warehouse compute became abundant and separable from storage, the industry flipped to ELT: load raw data first, transform inside the warehouse. dbt gave this pattern a standardized, code-first, version-controlled workflow, and popularized the 'analytics engineer' role that sits between data engineering and analytics.

whyItMatters.business: dbt shortens the path from raw data to trusted metrics: analysts can build and ship reliable, tested datasets themselves, so decisions are based on consistent definitions of 'revenue' or 'active user' rather than conflicting spreadsheets.
whyItMatters.engineering: It brings software-engineering practices - version control, modularity, code review, automated testing, and CI - to SQL transformations that used to live in ad-hoc scripts and stored procedures, drastically reducing breakage and rework.
whyItMatters.scalability: Because dbt pushes computation into the warehouse and parallelizes independent models via the DAG, the same project scales from a handful of models to thousands without changing the workflow, leveraging the warehouse's elastic compute.
whyItMatters.cost: ELT with dbt avoids maintaining a separate transformation cluster; you pay only for warehouse compute you already run, and dbt's materialization choices (view vs table vs incremental) let you tune spend precisely.
whyItMatters.reliability: Tests, a deterministic DAG build order, and reproducible SQL make pipelines predictable and debuggable; a failing test can stop a build before bad data reaches dashboards, improving trust in reporting.

coreComponents.name: Models (SQL SELECT files)
coreComponents.definition: A model is a single .sql file containing one SELECT statement; dbt wraps it in CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS and materializes it in the warehouse.
coreComponents.purpose: To define a transformation declaratively - you describe the desired result set, and dbt manages how it becomes a database object.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Encapsulate one logical transformation, reference upstream data via ref()/source(), and stay idempotent so it can be rebuilt safely.

coreComponents.name: Jinja templating (ref / source / macros)
coreComponents.definition: dbt SQL is templated with Jinja; functions like {{ ref('model') }} and {{ source('schema','table') }} resolve to fully qualified table names at compile time.
coreComponents.purpose: To create dependencies between models without hard-coding database names, enabling the DAG, environment portability, and reuse via macros.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Express dependencies, inject configuration, and let one codebase target dev/prod schemas by swapping compiled references.

coreComponents.name: The warehouse adapter and target
coreComponents.definition: An adapter is a plugin (e.g., dbt-snowflake, dbt-bigquery, dbt-postgres) that translates dbt's compiled SQL/DDL into dialect-specific commands and connects to a configured target.
coreComponents.purpose: To let one dbt project run against different warehouses and environments by changing connection profiles, not model code.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Open the warehouse connection, execute compiled DDL/DML, and handle dialect differences in materialization logic.
coreComponents.examples: profiles.yml target: dev on Snowflake | prod on BigQuery

internalWorking: You write models as SELECT statements and configuration as YAML; when you run dbt, it parses every file and resolves Jinja, turning {{ ref('x') }} into the real, environment-specific table name for model x.

From those resolved references dbt builds a DAG - a directed acyclic graph where each node is a model and each edge is a dependency - which encodes the exact order models must be built and which can run in parallel.

For each model dbt generates the appropriate DDL/DML based on its materialization (CREATE VIEW AS SELECT, CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, or an incremental MERGE) and sends that SQL to the warehouse over the adapter connection.
The warehouse executes the transformation using its own compute and storage - dbt itself does not process rows; it orchestrates SQL and never moves data out of the warehouse.

After building, dbt can run tests (also compiled to SELECT queries that should return zero failing rows) and generate documentation and lineage from the same parsed graph, giving a reproducible, observable build.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Sources (raw loaded tables) -> dbt parses models + resolves ref()/source() -> DAG built -> compiled SQL (CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT) -> warehouse executes in dependency order -> transformed models (staging -> marts) -> tests + docs -> BI / analytics consumers
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. An ingestion tool (Fivetran, Airbyte, a custom loader) extracts data from a source system and loads it raw into the warehouse, e.g. raw.orders and raw.customers.
2. dbt declares those raw tables as sources in a YAML file so models can reference them safely via {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}.
3. A staging model stg_orders selects from the source, renames columns, casts types, and does light cleanup, materialized as a view.
4. A mart model fct_orders selects from {{ ref('stg_orders') }} and {{ ref('stg_customers') }}, joining and aggregating into a business-ready fact table.
5. dbt orders the build - sources first, then staging, then marts - runs tests on the outputs, and the finished fct_orders is queried by BI tools, all without data ever leaving the warehouse.

keyTerminology.meaning: ELT loads raw data into the warehouse first and transforms it there; ETL transforms data in an external engine before loading. dbt is the T in ELT.
keyTerminology.importance: Understanding ELT explains dbt's whole design: it never moves data out, it just orchestrates SQL run by the warehouse.

keyTerminology.meaning: A single SQL SELECT file that dbt materializes as a table or view in the warehouse.
keyTerminology.importance: Models are the fundamental unit of work in dbt; everything - dependencies, tests, docs - is organized around them.

keyTerminology.meaning: A role that applies software-engineering practices (version control, testing, modularity) to analytics transformations, typically using dbt.
keyTerminology.importance: dbt popularized this role; it explains who dbt is built for and why it emphasizes engineering rigor over point-and-click ETL.

keyTerminology.meaning: Running transformations as SQL inside the data warehouse using its own compute, rather than in a separate processing tier.
keyTerminology.importance: This is the core efficiency of dbt/ELT: no extra cluster to maintain and elastic scaling comes for free from the warehouse.

importantConcepts.concept: Why ELT replaced ETL for analytics
importantConcepts.explanation: What: ELT flips the order to Extract, Load, then Transform. Why: cloud warehouses decoupled cheap elastic storage from powerful on-demand compute, so it became cheaper and simpler to load raw data and transform it in place than to run a separate transformation cluster. How: ingestion tools land raw data, then dbt runs SQL transformations inside the warehouse. Pitfall: teams sometimes still pre-transform in the loader, losing the raw source of truth - in ELT you keep raw data immutable so you can always reprocess and audit.

importantConcepts.concept: dbt orchestrates SQL, it does not process data
importantConcepts.explanation: What: dbt compiles your SELECTs into DDL and hands them to the warehouse to execute. Why: this keeps huge datasets where they already live and uses the warehouse's optimized, parallel engine instead of a Python process. How: the adapter opens a connection and issues CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT statements. Pitfall: beginners expect dbt to 'run' fast locally with lots of data - performance is entirely the warehouse's; dbt only sends SQL, so tuning means tuning warehouse queries and materializations.

importantConcepts.concept: SQL-as-code with version control and tests
importantConcepts.explanation: What: dbt treats transformations as code in a git repo with automated tests. Why: analytics logic used to live in undocumented, untested stored procedures and dashboards that silently broke. How: models, tests, and docs are files you review, version, and run in CI before merging. Pitfall: skipping tests and documentation because 'it works now' - the value of dbt compounds only when you actually add tests and keep models modular.

variationsAndTypes: **dbt Core:** the free, open-source command-line tool you run yourself (locally, in CI, or via an orchestrator like Airflow/Dagster).
**dbt Cloud:** dbt Labs' hosted platform adding a browser IDE, job scheduler, hosted docs, and CI integrations on top of dbt Core.
**ELT vs ETL:** ELT (dbt) transforms inside the warehouse; ETL transforms in an external engine before load.
**Warehouse adapters:** dbt-snowflake, dbt-bigquery, dbt-redshift, dbt-postgres, dbt-databricks - the same project runs on different backends.
**Transformation-only scope:** dbt does not extract or load; it pairs with ingestion tools (Fivetran, Airbyte) for E and L, and orchestrators for scheduling.
advantages: **Engineering rigor for SQL:** version control, modularity, code review, and automated testing come standard, replacing brittle ad-hoc scripts.
**Warehouse-native and scalable:** transformations run on the warehouse's elastic compute, so projects scale without a separate transformation cluster.
**Automatic dependency management:** the DAG orders and parallelizes builds from ref()/source(), so you never hand-code run order.
**Built-in documentation and lineage:** dbt generates browsable docs and a lineage graph from the same code, keeping knowledge current.
disadvantages: **SQL-centric:** logic that is awkward in SQL (complex procedural work, ML) does not fit dbt well and needs other tools.
**Warehouse required:** dbt depends on a running warehouse; you cannot transform without one, and warehouse costs/quirks apply.
**Not an orchestrator or ingestion tool:** dbt only does T, so you still need scheduling and EL tooling around it.
**Learning curve:** Jinja templating, materializations, and project structure take time to learn for analysts new to engineering practices.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use dbt when your data already lands (or can land) in a cloud data warehouse and you want tested, version-controlled, modular SQL transformations shared across a team - the standard modern analytics-engineering setup.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid dbt as your only tool for heavy procedural logic, real-time streaming transforms, or ML pipelines, and do not expect it to handle extraction/loading or scheduling by itself - pair it with the right E/L and orchestration tools.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Imagine a restaurant. In old-style ETL, ingredients were prepped in a separate off-site kitchen and then trucked in - slow and expensive. ELT delivers raw ingredients straight into the restaurant's own well-equipped kitchen (the warehouse) and preps them right there. dbt is the head chef with a book of recipes (models): each recipe is a simple statement of the finished dish, the chef knows which dishes depend on which prep steps (the DAG), cooks them in the right order using the restaurant's own ovens, and tastes each dish (tests) before it goes out to diners (BI dashboards).

commonMisconceptions.myth: dbt is a database or a data-processing engine that moves and crunches your data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: dbt does not store or process rows itself. It compiles SQL and orchestrates it; all data storage and computation happen inside your warehouse, which dbt simply sends CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT statements to.

commonMisconceptions.myth: dbt handles the whole pipeline including extracting and loading data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: dbt only does the Transform step of ELT. Extraction and loading are done by ingestion tools, and scheduling is done by an orchestrator; dbt assumes raw data is already in the warehouse.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You need to be a software engineer to use dbt.
commonMisconceptions.reality: dbt is designed for people who know SQL. Models are just SELECT statements; the engineering practices (git, tests, modularity) are learnable habits layered on top, which is exactly the analytics-engineer skill set dbt enables.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Because transformation runs in the warehouse, scaling means scaling warehouse compute (larger virtual warehouses/slots) and using the DAG's parallelism; incremental materializations keep large models from full-rebuilding every run.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Deterministic DAG ordering and reproducible compiled SQL make builds repeatable; tests gate bad data, and re-running a model is idempotent because dbt recreates the object from its SELECT.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: A failing model stops its downstream dependents (dbt tracks the graph), so bad data does not silently propagate; you can rerun from the point of failure with selectors.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track run duration per model, test pass/fail counts, freshness of sources, and warehouse cost per run; dbt emits run artifacts (run_results.json) you can pipe to monitoring.
productionConsiderations.security: Warehouse credentials live in profiles/secrets, not code; permissions are managed in the warehouse (role-based access), and dbt runs with a service role scoped to the schemas it manages.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Choose materializations deliberately (views for cheap logic, tables for reused heavy logic, incremental for large append-heavy data) and schedule runs to match data freshness needs rather than running constantly.
productionConsiderations.performance: Performance is warehouse SQL performance: push down filters early in staging, avoid unnecessary table materializations, and let dbt parallelize independent models via thread configuration.

codeExamples.title: A minimal ELT flow: source -> staging model -> mart model
codeExamples.overview: Two dbt models showing how raw loaded data is referenced via source() and ref() to build a clean fact table entirely with SQL SELECTs.
codeExamples.code:
-- models/staging/stg_orders.sql
-- Staging model: clean and standardize raw orders (materialized as a view)
{{ config(materialized='view') }}

select
    id                         as order_id,
    customer_id,
    lower(status)              as status,
    amount_cents / 100.0       as order_amount,
    cast(created_at as date)   as order_date
from {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}   -- raw table loaded by ingestion tool
where status is not null


-- models/marts/fct_daily_revenue.sql
-- Mart model: aggregate clean orders into daily revenue (materialized as a table)
{{ config(materialized='table') }}

select
    order_date,
    count(*)              as num_orders,
    sum(order_amount)     as total_revenue
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}          -- depends on the staging model
where status = 'completed'
group by order_date
order by order_date
codeExamples.breakdown: stg_orders reads directly from a declared source (raw.orders) and does light cleaning, materialized as a view (cheap, always fresh). fct_daily_revenue reads from {{ ref('stg_orders') }} - this ref() both fetches the correct table name and tells dbt that fct_daily_revenue depends on stg_orders, so dbt builds staging first. The config() blocks set how each model is materialized. Notice there is no CREATE TABLE text - dbt adds that around your SELECT.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: After 'dbt run', the warehouse contains a view analytics.stg_orders and a table analytics.fct_daily_revenue with columns order_date, num_orders, total_revenue - one row per day.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Referencing a raw table directly (from raw.orders) instead of using source() breaks lineage and environment portability. Forgetting that ref() creates a dependency leads to surprise build-order behavior if you bypass it.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep staging as views (cheap, one per source table) and materialize reused, heavy aggregations like fct_daily_revenue as tables so downstream queries are fast.

codeExamples.title: Declaring sources and running the project (YAML + CLI)
codeExamples.overview: The YAML that registers raw tables as sources plus the command-line workflow to build and inspect the project.
codeExamples.code:
# models/staging/_sources.yml
version: 2

sources:
  - name: raw                 # logical name used in {{ source('raw', ...) }}
    database: analytics_db    # where the loaded raw data lives
    schema: raw
    tables:
      - name: orders
      - name: customers
codeExamples.breakdown: This file registers the raw schema and its tables as dbt 'sources'. The name 'raw' is what you pass to {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}. Declaring sources centralizes where raw data lives, makes lineage explicit, and lets dbt test source freshness. Changing the database/schema here (per environment) re-points every model without editing SQL.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: dbt now recognizes source('raw','orders') and source('raw','customers'); they appear as green source nodes at the top of the lineage graph in dbt docs.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Mismatched database/schema names cause 'relation not found' errors at run time. Omitting version: 2 at the top of the YAML makes dbt reject the file.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Group sources by system and add freshness checks so dbt can warn when raw data is stale before you build models on top of it.

codeExamples.title: Building the project from the command line
codeExamples.overview: The core dbt CLI commands that compile, build, and document a project against the warehouse.
codeExamples.code:
# Check the connection to the warehouse defined in profiles.yml
dbt debug

# Compile SQL and build all models (runs CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT)
dbt run

# Run models AND their tests in dependency order
dbt build

# Build just one model and everything downstream of it
dbt run --select stg_orders+

# Generate and serve browsable documentation + lineage graph
dbt docs generate
dbt docs serve
codeExamples.breakdown: dbt debug verifies credentials and connectivity first. dbt run materializes every model in DAG order. dbt build runs models and their tests together (the recommended production command). The --select flag with the + operator targets a model and its downstream dependents. dbt docs generate + serve builds an interactive site with descriptions and the lineage DAG.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Running 'dbt run':
15:04:12  Running with dbt=1.9.0
15:04:13  Found 2 models, 1 source
15:04:15  1 of 2 OK created sql view model analytics.stg_orders ... [OK in 0.9s]
15:04:16  2 of 2 OK created sql table model analytics.fct_daily_revenue [OK in 1.4s]
15:04:16  Completed successfully
15:04:16  Done. PASS=2 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=2
codeExamples.commonIssues: Running dbt without a valid profiles.yml target causes a connection error (fix with dbt debug). Running 'dbt run' but expecting tests to execute - you need 'dbt test' or 'dbt build' for that.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use 'dbt build' in production so tests run alongside models, and use --select to rebuild only what changed instead of the whole project.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An e-commerce company loads raw orders and customers into Snowflake via Fivetran, but analysts define 'revenue' inconsistently across dashboards. The company wants one trusted, tested, daily-revenue dataset built with modular, version-controlled SQL.
endToEndExample.inputData: Raw tables landed by Fivetran: raw.orders (id, customer_id, status, amount_cents, created_at) and raw.customers (id, region, signup_date), refreshed hourly, with occasional nulls and mixed-case status values.
endToEndExample.architecture: Fivetran handles Extract + Load into Snowflake. dbt declares raw as sources, builds staging views (stg_orders, stg_customers), then a mart table fct_daily_revenue. Airflow triggers 'dbt build' on a schedule; BI tools read the mart.
processingSteps: 1. Fivetran loads raw.orders and raw.customers into Snowflake (the E and L of ELT).
2. dbt registers those tables as sources in _sources.yml, making the raw layer explicit and testable.
3. Staging models clean and standardize each source (rename, cast, lowercase status) as views via {{ source(...) }}.
4. The mart model fct_daily_revenue aggregates completed orders by day, reading via {{ ref('stg_orders') }} so dbt builds staging first.
5. 'dbt build' runs models plus tests (not_null, accepted_values) in DAG order; on success, dashboards query the single fct_daily_revenue table.
endToEndExample.output: A Snowflake table analytics.fct_daily_revenue with one row per day (order_date, num_orders, total_revenue), rebuilt on schedule and validated by tests, serving as the single source of truth for revenue.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Airflow tracks job success/failure; dbt run_results.json records per-model timing and test outcomes; source freshness checks warn if Fivetran data is stale; Snowflake query history tracks compute cost per run.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If a test fails (e.g., an unexpected status value), dbt build marks the model as errored and skips downstream models so bad revenue never reaches dashboards; the run is rerun after the data issue is fixed.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Every dashboard now reads the same tested revenue definition, built by reviewed SQL in git; a change to the revenue logic is made in one model, code-reviewed, tested in CI, and propagates everywhere - eliminating the conflicting-numbers problem.

industryUseCases.company: Consumer subscription apps (e.g., media/streaming analytics teams)
industryUseCases.problem: Dozens of analysts wrote overlapping SQL to compute active-user and churn metrics, producing inconsistent numbers across teams.
industryUseCases.solution: Centralize metric logic in dbt models with tests and documentation, built from raw event data loaded into the warehouse.
industryUseCases.benefits: One consistent, tested definition of each metric, version-controlled and code-reviewed, ending dashboard disagreements.

industryUseCases.problem: Raw order and inventory data loaded by ingestion tools needed reliable daily transformation into finance-grade reporting tables.
industryUseCases.solution: dbt staging + mart layers on Snowflake/BigQuery, scheduled via an orchestrator, with source freshness and data tests.
industryUseCases.benefits: Finance-trusted daily numbers built warehouse-natively, with lineage that shows exactly how each figure was derived.

industryUseCases.problem: Product, sales, and support data lived in silos with no shared, tested transformation layer feeding the BI tool.
industryUseCases.solution: A single dbt project transforming loaded raw data into conformed dimensions and facts, with docs auto-generated for stakeholders.
industryUseCases.benefits: Faster analyst onboarding via documentation and lineage, fewer broken dashboards, and a scalable, reviewable transformation codebase.

productionDeepDive.scalability: dbt scales by scaling the warehouse and exploiting DAG parallelism (threads); large projects use incremental models so heavy tables process only new rows rather than full rebuilds each run.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: The dependency graph ensures a failed upstream model skips its dependents, preventing bad data from propagating; runs are idempotent and can be re-executed or resumed with selectors like --select state:modified+.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Availability rests on the managed cloud warehouse (highly available by design) and the orchestrator; dbt itself is a stateless build step that can rerun anywhere with the same repo and credentials.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because models are code and warehouses keep raw sources immutable, the entire transformed layer can be rebuilt from scratch by re-running the dbt project against retained raw data.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Tune warehouse SQL (filter early in staging, avoid needless table materializations), increase threads for parallel model builds, and use incremental materializations to cut compute on large tables.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Match materializations to usage (views for light/rare logic, tables for reused heavy logic, incremental for big append-heavy data) and schedule runs to real freshness needs to avoid paying for constant recomputation.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Store warehouse credentials in a secrets manager, run dbt under a least-privilege service role scoped to its schemas, and rely on the warehouse's role-based access control for data governance.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Ingest dbt artifacts (run_results.json, manifest.json) into monitoring to track model timings, test failures, and lineage; add source freshness checks and alert on failed builds or slow models.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Use dbt tests (not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships) to validate outputs on every build, and fail the build when critical tests fail so bad data never reaches consumers.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: dbt logs each model and test result; wire the orchestrator to alert on run failures and test errors, and surface source freshness warnings so stale upstream data is caught early.

recommendedPractices: **Always reference upstream data with ref() and source()**, never hard-coded table names, so lineage and environment portability work.
**Layer your models** into staging (one per source, light cleaning) and marts (business logic) for clarity and reuse.
**Add tests and documentation** to models from the start; the value of dbt compounds only when outputs are validated and described.
**Keep raw data immutable** and do all transformation in dbt so you can always reprocess and audit from the source of truth.
engineeringStandards: Version-control the whole dbt project in git and require code review before merging model changes.
Run 'dbt build' (models + tests) in CI on pull requests to catch breakage before it reaches production.
Use one model per file with a single SELECT and let materialization be a config, not hand-written DDL.
designRecommendations: Adopt a staging -> intermediate -> marts folder structure so responsibilities are clear and models stay small.
Declare every raw table as a source and never let a model select from a raw relation directly.
Choose materializations intentionally per model rather than defaulting everything to table or view.
namingConventions: Prefix staging models with stg_ (e.g., stg_orders) and mart facts/dimensions with fct_/dim_ (e.g., fct_orders, dim_customers).
Name source YAML entries by source system and table so {{ source('raw','orders') }} reads clearly.
Use consistent, snake_case, business-friendly column names in staging (order_id, order_amount) so downstream models are readable.
documentationStandards: Describe each model and its key columns in schema YAML so 'dbt docs' produces a useful catalog.
Document the meaning of business metrics (how 'revenue' or 'active user' is defined) alongside the model that produces them.
Keep the lineage graph meaningful by using ref()/source() everywhere so docs show the true dependency flow.
testingStrategies: Add generic tests (not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships) to primary keys and critical columns.
Run source freshness checks so stale raw data is caught before models build on it.
Gate production builds on tests via 'dbt build' so failing data quality stops the pipeline instead of shipping bad numbers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hard-coding raw table names in models instead of using source() and ref().
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is the fastest way to get a query working, and analysts new to dbt write SQL the way they always have.
commonMistakes.impact: Broken lineage, no build-order guarantees, and models that fail when promoted to a different environment/schema.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Reference raw tables via {{ source(...) }} and other models via {{ ref(...) }} so dbt builds the DAG, orders builds, and stays portable across environments.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating dbt as an ETL tool that also extracts and loads data.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Beginners see dbt manage the pipeline and assume it does the whole job end to end.
commonMistakes.impact: Confusion when dbt cannot pull from source systems; wasted effort trying to make dbt do extraction it was never designed for.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use ingestion tools for E and L and an orchestrator for scheduling; scope dbt to the Transform step on data already in the warehouse.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping tests and documentation because models 'already work'.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Delivering a working query feels done, and tests/docs seem like optional overhead under deadline pressure.
commonMistakes.impact: Silent data-quality regressions and undocumented logic that breaks trust and slows every future change.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Add tests and column/model descriptions as part of building each model, and enforce them in CI so quality is a standard, not an afterthought.

comparisonSection.explanation: ELT loads raw data into the warehouse first and transforms it there using warehouse compute, keeping an immutable raw layer you can always reprocess. ETL transforms in a separate engine before loading, which was necessary when warehouse compute was scarce/expensive but adds a cluster to maintain and loses the raw source of truth. Modern cloud warehouses make ELT cheaper, simpler, and the default for analytics, which is exactly where dbt fits.

dbt Core is the free command-line tool you run yourself - locally, in CI, or via an orchestrator - giving full control and no per-seat cost but requiring you to manage scheduling, environments, and docs hosting. dbt Cloud wraps Core with a browser IDE, managed scheduler, hosted documentation, and CI integrations, trading cost for convenience and lower operational burden. Both run the same underlying transformation engine and project structure.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is dbt and what problem does it solve?
beginnerQuestions.answer: dbt (data build tool) is a transformation framework that lets you define data transformations as SQL SELECT statements, which it compiles and runs inside a data warehouse. It solves the problem of ad-hoc, untested, un-versioned analytics SQL by bringing software-engineering practices - version control, modularity via ref(), testing, and documentation - to the Transform step of ELT.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress that dbt handles only the T of ELT and orchestrates SQL rather than processing data itself. Mentioning tests and version control shows you understand its real value beyond 'running SQL'.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?
beginnerQuestions.answer: In ETL, data is Extracted, Transformed in a separate engine, then Loaded into the warehouse. In ELT, data is Extracted, Loaded raw into the warehouse first, then Transformed there using the warehouse's own compute. dbt implements the Transform in ELT, which became standard once cloud warehouses made compute cheap and elastic.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Explain the 'why': decoupled, cheap warehouse compute made in-warehouse transformation practical, and keeping raw data immutable lets you reprocess and audit.

intermediateQuestions.question: Does dbt store or process your data? Explain what actually happens when you run it.
intermediateQuestions.answer: No. dbt does not store or process rows. When you run it, dbt parses your models, resolves Jinja like ref()/source(), builds a DAG, and generates DDL/DML (CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT) that it sends over an adapter to the warehouse. The warehouse executes the SQL using its own compute; dbt only orchestrates.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This distinguishes candidates who understand dbt's architecture. Emphasize that performance tuning means tuning warehouse SQL and materializations, not dbt itself.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does dbt know what order to build models in?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Through ref() and source(). Each {{ ref('other_model') }} declares a dependency, so dbt builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from these references. It then builds upstream models before downstream ones and runs independent branches in parallel. You never hand-code the order.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tie the DAG to the reason ref() exists: it does double duty, resolving the table name and declaring the dependency.

advancedQuestions.question: Where does dbt fit in a modern data stack, and what does it explicitly not do?
advancedQuestions.answer: dbt is the transformation layer. Upstream, ingestion tools (Fivetran, Airbyte) do Extract and Load; dbt then transforms raw data into staging and mart layers; downstream, BI tools consume the results, and an orchestrator (Airflow, Dagster, dbt Cloud scheduler) schedules dbt runs. dbt explicitly does not extract, load, or schedule itself.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Showing the surrounding tools proves you understand dbt's boundaries and can architect a full pipeline, not just write models.

advancedQuestions.question: How does dbt bring software-engineering practices to analytics, and why does it matter at scale?
advancedQuestions.answer: Models are code in a git repo, so you get version control, code review, and CI. ref()/source() give modularity and lineage. Tests validate outputs on every build, and docs are generated from the same code. At scale this prevents the silent breakage and inconsistent metrics that plague thousands of ad-hoc queries, and lets many people safely collaborate on one transformation codebase.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Connect each practice to a concrete failure it prevents (broken dashboards, conflicting numbers) to show real-world understanding.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your team has raw data loaded into Snowflake by Fivetran, but every analyst computes 'monthly revenue' slightly differently, so leadership sees conflicting numbers. How would you use dbt to fix this?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The root cause is duplicated, un-shared logic. dbt centralizes it: declare the raw tables as sources, build staging models to standardize them, then one mart model that defines revenue once. Add tests and docs, version-control it, and point all dashboards at the single mart.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Create a dbt project: register raw.orders as a source; build stg_orders to clean/standardize; build a fct_monthly_revenue mart that encodes the single agreed revenue definition using {{ ref('stg_orders') }}. Add not_null/accepted_values tests and column docs, run 'dbt build' in CI, and migrate all dashboards to read the one mart. Now revenue is defined once, tested, reviewed, and consistent everywhere.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the transformation layer for a company that loads raw operational data into a cloud warehouse and needs reliable, tested reporting datasets for BI.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use dbt on top of the warehouse. Declare all raw tables as sources; build a staging layer (one view per source, light cleaning), optional intermediate models, and a marts layer (facts/dimensions with business logic). Reference everything via ref()/source() to form the DAG. Add generic tests and docs, and schedule 'dbt build' via an orchestrator.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: ELT-in-warehouse keeps things simple and scalable but ties you to warehouse compute cost and SQL's limits; layering adds structure at the cost of more models to maintain. Materialization choices trade freshness vs cost.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Increase warehouse size and dbt threads for parallelism, convert large tables to incremental materializations, and use --select state:modified+ in CI to build only what changed. Partition the project into well-named domains as it grows.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: dbt is a warehouse-native transformation framework that turns modular, version-controlled SQL SELECTs into tested tables/views, implementing the Transform step of ELT.
keyConcepts: dbt does the T in ELT: raw data is loaded first, then transformed inside the warehouse.
Models are SQL SELECTs; dbt wraps them in CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS and materializes them.
ref() and source() declare dependencies, forming the DAG that orders builds.
dbt orchestrates SQL - the warehouse does all storage and computation.
Brings version control, testing, and documentation to analytics SQL.
commands: dbt run          # build all models (CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT)
dbt build        # run models + tests in DAG order (recommended)
dbt run --select stg_orders+   # build a model and its downstream
dbt docs generate && dbt docs serve   # build and view docs + lineage
interviewPoints: ELT vs ETL and why ELT won with cloud warehouses.
dbt only transforms; it does not extract, load, or schedule.
ref()/source() build the DAG and enable environment portability.
dbt compiles SQL; the warehouse executes it.
Value = engineering rigor (git, tests, docs) on top of SQL.
quickNotes: Pair dbt with ingestion tools (Fivetran/Airbyte) and an orchestrator (Airflow/Dagster).
dbt Core is the free CLI; dbt Cloud is the hosted platform.
Keep raw data immutable so you can always reprocess.
Materialization (view/table/incremental) is a config, not hand-written DDL.

keyTakeaways: dbt is the Transform layer of ELT: raw data is loaded into a cloud warehouse first, and dbt transforms it in place using the warehouse's own compute, never moving data out.
You write transformations as simple SQL SELECT models; dbt wraps them in CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT and materializes them, so you describe the result and dbt manages the how.
ref() and source() are central: they resolve real table names and declare dependencies, from which dbt builds a DAG that orders and parallelizes builds automatically.
dbt's core value is bringing software engineering to analytics - version control, modularity, automated tests, and generated documentation - replacing brittle, inconsistent ad-hoc SQL.
dbt is only the T: it relies on ingestion tools for extract/load and an orchestrator for scheduling, and all performance and cost ultimately come from the underlying warehouse.
